articles.title: Alberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
articles.summary: The overwhelming vote by Alberta to stay in Canada gives Mark Carney political capital to focus on remaking the country's economy, writes the BBC's Lyse Doucet.
articles.body:
"Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.

It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.

But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.

Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.

Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders.

Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."

Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too.

"Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.

Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".

Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.

The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls.

"I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."

In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.

And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.

But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast.

"Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto.

"Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build.

An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets – a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations.

At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night.

After Monday's vote, Carney – the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance – pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials.

'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism

Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat

"Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year.

At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes.

Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too.

The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union.

"I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel.

For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home – including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians would envy.

And the plain-speaking politician's strong and steady response to Trump threats, including retaliatory tariffs, has seen his star rising on the world stage. It's an unexpected turn for a country which has often been missing from top tables and has sometimes even been dismissed as "boring".

The Economist magazine decided to put Carney on their cover, on this week of weeks for Canada, with a perfect red maple leaf between his teeth.

"Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world," reads one of its headlines, with an article which also focuses on Canada's "vulnerabilities" including Alberta's ballot.

"The broader takeaway from this vote might be that Canadian unity is in fine shape," remarks David Moscrop, political scientist and author of the forthcoming book On Nationalism.

"But what happens after Donald Trump is gone and Canada no longer has a single, bombastic target which drives Canadians to rally around the flag?" he asks.

Carney's decision to recently walk away from trade talks with the US gave rise to another swell of Canadian pride and patriotism. But if this trade war drags on with a country which traditionally takes 70% of Canada's exports, Canadians will feel even greater pain in their daily lives.

But today is a day to vigorously wave the maple leaf flag.

"It's a win for Team Canada and its resilience," commented CBC journalist Janyce McGregor during the public broadcaster's rolling coverage of a vast country of never-ending building issues.

articles.title: In 2024, ‘Sister, Sister’ actress Tamera Mowry-Housley paid $3.8 million for a neglected 15-acre Napa Valley property; while planning an orchard and vineyard, she listed her longtime California home for $2.69 million
articles.summary: Actress Tamera Mowry-Housley and her husband, former journalist Adam Housley, are preparing for a new chapter in Napa Valley as they put their longtime
articles.body: Actress Tamera Mowry-Housley and her husband, former journalist Adam Housley, are preparing for a new chapter in Napa Valley as they put their longtime Fairfield, California, home on the market for $2.69 million. The June 2026 listing follows their $3.8 million purchase of a neglected wine-country property in October 2024, a move detailed by Realtor dot com and People as the couple documents their renovation journey online. The transition marks a shift from a spacious suburban residence to a rural property where the family hopes to grow its own produce, establish an orchard and vineyard, and embrace a more sustainable lifestyle.A longtime family home goes on the marketThe Fairfield residence, which the couple purchased for approximately $1.4 million in 2011, has five bedrooms and five bathrooms across about 4,863 square feet, according to the listing coverage. Built in 2005, the home sits on a roughly half-acre lot north of San Francisco.Its features include an open-plan living area, high ceilings, a fireplace, an upgraded kitchen with professional-grade appliances and custom cabinetry, and a primary bedroom with French doors opening onto a balcony. Outside, landscaped grounds, a saltwater swimming pool and views of the surrounding hills give the property a resort-like feel.The asking price of $2.69 million represents a substantial increase over the couple’s original purchase price, although the eventual sale price will depend on market conditions and negotiations. Real estate agents Ryan Nemeyer and Alfonso Garcia of the Nemeyer Garcia Team at Engel & Völkers are handling the listing. The agents have highlighted the home’s privacy, outdoor space and access to nearby employment centres as selling points for prospective buyers.Why the couple chose Napa ValleyThe move follows years of searching for a countryside property that could accommodate the family’s ambitions beyond city living. In October 2024, Mowry-Housley and her husband bought a Napa Valley estate for $3.8 million. Unlike their Fairfield home, the new property was in need of extensive renovation. The single-storey residence measures approximately 2,718 square feet and has three bedrooms and three bathrooms. It had reportedly been vacant since 2018.The couple’s decision was driven largely by the land rather than the existing house. The estate spans roughly 15 acres and includes a natural pond, wooded areas and more than four acres of Cabernet Sauvignon vines, according to the property’s previous listing. Adam Housley has described the setting as central to their plans, with the family hoping to create a home that reflects their own design preferences while allowing them to spend more time outdoors.Renovating a neglected estate into a dream homeThe couple began documenting the transformation in April 2026 through their YouTube series, The Housley Farm: Building Our Dream Home. The project offers viewers a look at the challenges of renovating a property that needs significant work while preserving the appeal of its natural surroundings.Their plans include developing an orchard and vineyard, keeping chickens and exploring ways to live more sustainably. The property’s pond is another feature they hope to make better use of as the renovation progresses. For Mowry-Housley, who rose to fame alongside her twin sister Tia Mowry in the sitcom Sister, Sister, the move also represents a personal adjustment. She has spoken about feeling excited about country life while acknowledging that leaving familiar urban surroundings is a significant change. The couple, who married in 2011, share two children, son Aden and daughter Ariah. Their new property is intended to give the family more room to connect with nature and build a lifestyle around the land.A different vision of family livingThe sale of the Fairfield home and the Napa renovation reflect a deliberate change in priorities. Their former residence offered extensive indoor space, established landscaping and a pool, while the new estate provides acreage and the opportunity to shape a property around farming, outdoor activities and family life.The Napa project remains a work in progress, and the listing of the Fairfield home does not itself confirm a completed sale. But the couple’s plans point towards a longer-term commitment to country living, with the land, rather than the house alone, at the centre of their next chapter.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Bill Ackman sounds off on 'crazy, radicalized' Democratic Party, argues it's in 'worst place it's ever been'
articles.summary: Investor Bill Ackman slammed the Democratic Party as "radicalized and anti-American," singling out Sen. Chuck Schumer for compromising his values to keep his job.
articles.body: Investor Bill Ackman called the Democratic Party "crazy, radicalized and anti-American" during an interview on Tuesday, arguing that the party is "in a very bad place." "I think the Democratic Party is in the worst place it's ever been, in the 250-year history of the country," Ackman told Katie Miller, host of the "Katie Miller Podcast." "I think it's become like this crazy, radicalized, you know, anti-American thing. I think it's — and by the way, I think there's some very high-quality Democrats, you know, senators and, sure, some congressmen — but the party itself, I think, is in a very bad place." Ackman specifically named Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., as someone he used to be friendly with but now believes has "compromised" on his values. FORMER BERNIE SANDERS OPERATIVE WARNS RADICAL LEFT HAS 'OVERTAKEN' THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY FROM WITHIN "And I think the problem with people who've chosen to be a politician for a career, you either have to get with the party in order to continue, or you get primaries," Ackman said. "You know, actually, Senator Schumer, I had a good relationship with him over the years. I thought he was a good man. But in recent years, I felt he's just trying to keep his job." "And, you know, that's the really low point for politicians when they'll compromise on their values, and they'll support, you know, a quasi-terrorist, perhaps running for Senate in Michigan, because they have to for the party," Ackman said. "Stuff like that to me is, or terrorist supporter, is not, that's, I find that pretty, deeply concerning." Schumer's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. "Chuck Schumer has been in Washington long enough to know exactly what’s happening to his party. The question isn’t whether he sees it. It’s whether he’s willing to do anything about it," Y. David Scharf, chair of Morrison Cohen’s government strategies and controversies practice, told Fox News Digital of Ackman's remarks. "There’s something remarkable about watching one of the most powerful Jewish Democrats in America struggle to stand up to the very people in his party who are alienating Jewish voters," he continued. "Bill Ackman isn’t asking Schumer to become a Republican. He’s asking him to act like the Democrat he spent decades telling us he was." EX-DSA MEMBER RIPS ABDUL EL-SAYED AND WARNS FAR-LEFT ADOPTING POLITICS OF FOREIGN TERROR ORG Ackman appeared to reference Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who has faced questions over his family's alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed's campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The controversy followed a Washington Free Beacon report about social media posts in which El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, described her family's history with the Muslim Brotherhood. In one 2012 post, Abdelhadi described a conversation with her and El-Sayed's mother, Fatten Elkomy, about her involvement with the organization during college in Egypt. "Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early '70s while she was in college #respect," she posted to X. El-Sayed has denied any family connections to the group. During a recent interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," El-Sayed rejected the assertions when asked to set the record straight. "I have no ties; we have no ties," El-Sayed said. During a town hall on Saturday, El-Sayed responded to a man identified as Tommy, asking him whether he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. "Sure," El-Sayed said. "Yeah, absolutely. But I want to ask the question that you're asking: Why are you asking the question?" ABDUL EL-SAYED GROWS AGITATED WITH REPORTER AFTER BEING PRESSED ON FAMILY'S ALLEGED MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES Ackman has also previously voiced his opposition to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, criticizing his policies as harmful to the city. "I'm not a fan," he responded. "He's very smart, very charismatic, very good at politics, but I think the decisions he's making are very bad for New York." articles.title: American Airlines jet suffers brake trouble, blown tire after landing at Chicago O'Hare: FAA
articles.summary: An American Airlines flight from Spain reported brake issues and a blown tire after landing at Chicago O'Hare on Tuesday.
articles.body: An American Airlines flight from Spain experienced brake issues and a blown tire after landing at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport on Tuesday afternoon. American Airlines Flight 41, a Boeing 787-800 traveling from Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat Airport in Spain, landed safely at O'Hare around 2:30 p.m. local time, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) told Fox News Digital in a statement. The FAA said the crew reported a brake issue followed by "a blown tire" after landing. DASHCAM VIDEO CAPTURES SMALL PLANE CRASHING ON SAN JOSE HIGHWAY, INJURING THREE ON BOARD, INCLUDING CHILD "Passengers deplaned via stairs and were bused to the terminal," the FAA said, adding that the agency "will investigate." The airline said 234 passengers and 11 crew members were aboard. American Airlines said first responders met the aircraft "out of an abundance of caution" and that passengers were safely transported to the terminal by bus. The airline said the aircraft has been taken out of service for inspection by its maintenance team and apologized to customers for the experience. articles.title: Tory MP questions government advisor's position after wife's Palestine Action post
articles.summary: A Downing Street spokeswoman told the BBC: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."
articles.body:
Conservative MP Alicia Kearns has raised concerns over whether Jonathan Powell, the National Security Advisor, can remain in his post following his wife's references to Palestine Action on social media.

The shadow home affairs minister has written to the prime minister questioning whether Powell's position is still tenable, despite the Metropolitan Police concluding no action was necessary over his wife's, Sarah Helm, comments.

A Downing Street spokeswoman told the BBC: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."

Posting on X last Thursday, Helm wrote: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action," responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney.

The Normal People writer announced last week that her books will not be supplied to UK booksellers after she announced she would use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

The Met investigation into Helm's post found "it did not meet the criminal threshold" and the matter was dropped on Saturday.

But Kearns has written to Andy Burnham about the handling of sensitive national security information, asking whether the government has investigated the posts and whether he retains full confidence in his adviser.

She told the BBC: "We cannot have the NSA's wife tweeting about what decisions her husband has or hasn't made."

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terror organisation last year, making it a a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years imprisonment to belong to or support the group.

An appeal against the proscription of Palestine Action is due to be heard by the Supreme Court next month , in a battle that has now gone on for more than year.

articles.title: UC Santa Barbara professor Edwina Barvosa sues University of California Regents over alleged gender discrimination, blocked promotions and $2.95 million pay gap with male colleague
articles.summary: Edwina Barvosa, a professor of social and political theory in the University of California, Santa Barbara’s Department of Feminist Studies, has filed a
articles.body: Edwina Barvosa, a professor of social and political theory in the University of California, Santa Barbara’s Department of Feminist Studies, has filed a lawsuit against the University of California Regents over alleged gender-based discrimination and unequal pay, The Daily Nexus reported.Barvosa, who has worked at UCSB since 1998, alleges that university administrators subjected her to discriminatory treatment, obstructed her academic advancement, denied her fair compensation and retaliated against her after she raised concerns about workplace practices.She is also affiliated with UCSB’s Department of Chicana and Chicano Studies and Department of Political Science.According to The Daily Nexus, the lawsuit was initially filed in June 2026 against the UC Regents, UC President James B. Milliken, Chancellor Dennis Assanis and other defendants. An amended complaint filed on August 31 named the UC Regents and unidentified defendants.The allegations have not been established in court. UCSB media spokesperson Kiki Reyes declined to comment, citing the pending litigation.Lawsuit alleges $2.95 million pay gap between Barvosa and male colleagueOne of the central claims in Barvosa’s lawsuit concerns her compensation compared with that of a male faculty member identified in the complaint as “Professor Y.”According to the complaint, as detailed by The Daily Nexus, Professor Y joined UCSB in 2006, eight years after Barvosa. The lawsuit states that Barvosa had approximately a decade more work experience than her male colleague.Despite what the complaint describes as similarities in their academic backgrounds and responsibilities, Barvosa alleges that she received approximately $2,957,526 less than Professor Y in base salary over the years they both worked at the university.The complaint also alleges that Professor Y was promoted more rapidly and was not held to the same career advancement standards as Barvosa and other female faculty members. It further disputes the relative assessment of their academic publications.According to the lawsuit, Barvosa approached the executive dean of UCSB’s College of Letters and Science to raise concerns about the alleged pay disparity. The complaint claims the dean acknowledged that she was underpaid but subsequently denied her a raise and promotion to full professor, citing academic requirements.Barvosa alleges that Professor Y had previously received a promotion despite not meeting the same standards.The lawsuit further claims that the alleged treatment was part of a broader pattern of discrimination against women within the University of California system and at UCSB.Professor alleges retaliation after raising discrimination concernsThe complaint outlines several instances in which Barvosa allegedly reported concerns about compensation, promotion and personnel review procedures to university administrators.In October 2018, she submitted a written complaint to Laury Oaks, then chair of the Department of Feminist Studies. According to the lawsuit, Barvosa raised concerns about inconsistent standards in compensation and promotion reviews, alleging that the practices disproportionately affected underrepresented minority faculty members.She continued to raise concerns between 2020 and 2022 through written complaints and verbal communications with university administrators.Barvosa alleges that, rather than addressing her concerns, UCSB administrators retaliated against her by assigning her what the complaint describes as punitive amounts of bureaucratic work and obstructing her academic research.The lawsuit argues that the alleged actions affected both her professional opportunities and her ability to advance her academic career.Lawsuit cites denied endowed chair position and research opportunityBarvosa’s complaint also details two incidents involving research and career advancement.In April 2021, she applied for the MacArthur Foundation UC Endowed Chair position, an academic appointment that the lawsuit describes as a significant career opportunity. According to the complaint, the university denied her application in June 2021 and offered the position to Professor Y instead.Barvosa alleges that she was equally or more qualified for the appointment than her male colleague.The complaint also describes an incident in June 2023, when UCSB’s Office of Research allegedly withheld approval for her participation in a research position at the University of Texas. The university reportedly cited alleged plagiarism in her research proposal.Barvosa disputes the accusation, describing it as baseless in the lawsuit, and claims that it damaged her professional reputation.These incidents form part of her broader allegations that university administrators obstructed her academic opportunities after she raised concerns about discrimination.Barvosa challenges denial of promotion and salary increaseThe lawsuit also addresses Barvosa’s 2025-26 merit review, during which she alleges she was denied a promotion and salary increase despite receiving unanimous support from her department.According to the complaint, the Department of Feminist Studies voted 9-0 in favour of advancing her from Professor IV to Professor V and recommended a corresponding salary increase.However, the Academic Senate Committee on Academic Personnel recommended neither advancement nor a raise, citing alleged deficiencies in research and teaching.Barvosa claims the conflicting recommendations reflect inconsistent standards in the university’s merit-review process. She also alleges that the decision was influenced by individuals who had previously shown hostility towards her complaints.The lawsuit seeks to challenge what Barvosa describes as unequal treatment in the evaluation of her academic work and career progression.Professor claims workplace conditions caused physical and emotional harmIn addition to alleging financial and professional losses, Barvosa claims that her treatment at UCSB caused significant physical and emotional harm.The complaint states that she suffered a stress-induced heart attack in December 2024, which she attributes to the strain of what she describes as unequal working conditions.These claims form part of her request for damages related to the alleged discrimination, harassment and retaliation.What is Edwina Barvosa seeking in her lawsuit?Barvosa is seeking compensation for lost wages, employment benefits, emotional distress and other damages.Her amended complaint outlines five causes of action, including alleged violations of California’s Equal Pay Act, discrimination, harassment and whistleblower retaliation.As reported by The Daily Nexus, the case centres on Barvosa’s allegations that UCSB subjected her to unequal compensation and career advancement practices and retaliated against her for reporting what she believed were discriminatory practices.UCSB spokesperson Kiki Reyes declined to comment on the allegations, citing the pending litigation. The claims remain allegations in a lawsuit, and the case’s outcome will depend on the legal proceedings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 2 British Indians assaulted during Dussehra, Bathukamma celebrations
articles.summary: LONDON: Two British Indian Telugu Hindu men were assaulted during a Dussehra and Bathukamma celebration in the town of Ossett, West Yorkshire, last
articles.body: LONDON: Two British Indian Telugu Hindu men were assaulted during a Dussehra and Bathukamma celebration in the town of Ossett, West Yorkshire, last Saturday night in what police believe was a racially aggravated attack. The assaults happened on Oct 17 outside Ossett Town Hall, which was hosting the celebration. The event was organised by local Telugu Hindu community groups.Earlier in the evening a group of around 25 local white youths, mostly male, were cycling around on e-bikes asking organisers what was going on in the town hall and who was inside. Some of them tried to force their way in, but security did not allow it.One of the victims, a 51-year-old British Indian man from the Hyderabad region, left the event at around 9pm and walked to his car with a friend. As they did so, they encountered a group of eight to 10 youths, some in black balaclavas.“One of them approached us and started asking us why we were here, what we were doing and looked aggressive,” he told TOI. “He circled around us and used filthy language. We didn’t respond. We didn’t feel it was safe to go further and started to go back to town hall and then he hit both of us. He hit me hard and pushed me to the ground on my face and left me bleeding. I stood up and then he punched me in my left eye … My friend was left with a head injury and his hand was bleeding.”There have been no arrests yet. Inspector Andrew Dickinson said: “We recognise the distress thishas caused to the wider Hindu community. We are treating these assaults seriously and are working to ensure those responsible are held accountable.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Convicted bank robber returns to old tricks with ‘old man’ mask in Florida heists, feds say
articles.summary: David Sartin Jr. allegedly robbed two Florida banks in a prosthetic "old man" mask weeks after starting supervised release from a 10-year bank robbery sentence.
articles.body: A convicted bank robber allegedly returned to a familiar disguise while robbing two Florida banks on supervised release, donning an "old man" mask and fleeing in a getaway vehicle tied to his earlier crimes, federal authorities said. David Sartin Jr., 40, of St. Petersburg, faces two bank robbery charges after investigators say he targeted banks weeks apart while concealing his face behind a prosthetic mask with gray facial hair. The allegations follow a sentence of more than 10 years in federal prison in a case involving five Texas bank robberies, during which Sartin wore a similar disguise, according to a criminal complaint reviewed by Fox News Digital. FLORIDA MEN INDICTED IN ARMED HOME INVASION WHERE SUSPECT POSED AS UTILITY WORKER, 13-YEAR-OLD ZIP-TIED: DOJ His supervised release began in May 2025. Investigators allege he robbed the first Florida bank in August 2026. "In all of SARTIN JR.’s bank robberies, he used a mask," an FBI special agent wrote in the affidavit. TWO KENTUCKY BANK EMPLOYEES SHOT AND KILLED DURING ROBBERY, POLICE HUNTING SUSPECT The first holdup happened Aug. 24 at Valley Bank in Largo, where the suspect entered wearing a straw hat, sports jacket, gloves and a prosthetic face covering, according to investigators. He approached a teller, demanded money and warned, "no dye packs," the complaint states. TEEN SUSPECT IN MURDER OF TWO BANK EMPLOYEES IN KENTUCKY LEADS POLICE ON WILD 130 MPH CHASE As the teller gathered cash and activated a silent alarm, the robber repeatedly urged the employee to hurry, a bank manager told investigators. "Until we meet again," the suspect said after collecting the money, according to the manager’s account. THIEF USES WAYMO AS A GETAWAY CAR Authorities say he escaped with $2,900, wedging a yellow wet-floor sign between the exit doors before fleeing toward a nearby church. Surveillance video showed the suspect retrieving a bicycle, riding into a nature preserve and leaving the area in a Toyota FJ Cruiser, according to the affidavit. FLOCK EXECUTIVE DEFENDS CRIME-FIGHTING CAMERAS AS ACLU ATTORNEY QUESTIONS COMPANY'S MOTIVES AMID BACKLASH Investigators traced the vehicle’s movements through video from surrounding businesses, city trucks, a police cruiser and a school bus. The Toyota was the same vehicle used in several of Sartin’s earlier Texas robberies, authorities said. On Sept. 15, a similarly disguised suspect entered a Truist Bank in St. Petersburg wearing a flat cap, glasses, a sports jacket and an "old man" mask with a gray mustache and whiskers. PHILADELPHIA MAN IN 'CHUCKY' MASK ACCUSED OF TERRORIZING CITIZENS NABBED IN LAS VEGAS AFTER MANHUNT He handed a teller a note demanding cash without dye and fled with approximately $2,554, according to the complaint. The teller suspected the man was wearing a mask and told investigators he "did not move like an old man would," the FBI agent wrote. THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC? By then, the FBI was monitoring Sartin’s home with a surveillance camera. Video captured the Toyota leaving before the second robbery and returning afterward, when a man resembling Sartin unloaded a bicycle, according to the affidavit. The following evening, investigators watched Sartin change the vehicle’s appearance. Investigators said he spray-painted the vehicle’s white roof black. MASKED SUSPECT CHARGED WITH USING FUEL, FIREWORKS IN WALMART KIDS SECTION AS COVER FOR MASSIVE JEWELRY HEIST Sartin was arrested Sept. 19 on a warrant for violating his supervised release. Searches uncovered a bicycle and clothing similar to those seen in the robbery video, authorities said. Agents searching his storage unit found an "old man" mask they said matched the disguise worn during both robberies, along with glasses, clothing and a fake handgun. In a guest room where Sartin occasionally stayed, investigators also found another mask and a journal identifying him as its author. Its title page included the words, "God’s Best friend is a Bank Robber!" according to the complaint. Sartin’s previous convictions stretch back nearly two decades. He was convicted of attempted bank robbery in Mississippi in 2008 following a failed holdup involving Halloween masks and disguises. In 2018, he was sentenced to 10 years and one month in federal prison in the Texas bank robbery case. articles.title: Parked cars barriers, leaning poles sentries on Chandigarh’s bicycle tracks.
articles.summary: Chandigarh’s 200-km bicycle tracks face illegal parking, vendors, broken streetlights and damaged kerbs, forcing cyclists into traffic and raising safety risks.
articles.body: Chandigarh: Broken lighting, illegal parking, and street vendors have turned the city’s sprawling 200-km bicycle network built at great public expense into a safety hazard.Mounting encroachments and maintenance lapses reflected in damaged kerbs have turned the track into an obstacle course for cyclists.City cyclist Ramnik Singh said: “The tracks are meant to provide cyclists with a safe, uninterrupted passage, but when vehicles, vendors, and other obstructions take over, we are forced to negotiate our way around them or move onto the main road, in the direct parth of fast traffic.”.Chandigarh began planning its extensive bicycle-track network in the early 2000s. In Dec 2002, the UT administration announced plans for almost 167 km of tracks along major V2 and V3 roads. Expansion gathered pace in 2017, followed by another 99 km approved for construction in Nov 2018.The network has since surpassed 200 km. While substantial public funds went into the infrastructure, residents note the primary challenge is maintaining accessibility and safety.Parking and Vending CongestionAlong Shanti Path, unauthorised vending, roadside storage of building materials, improper parking, and horticulture waste dumping have restricted movement. Damaged kerbs further compound the issue.Parking congestion is prevalent near Apni Mandi and the day market in Sector 43A on Jan Marg, Dhanas on Dakshin Marg, Sector 34B near Sarovar Path and V5 Road, and V4 roads in sectors 29, 40, and 46.“Poor parking management creates congestion and leaves little room for cyclists and pedestrians. Enforcement cannot be limited to occasional drives; it has to be regular,” said Rakesh Sharma of Sector 45.The positioning of certain vending sites has also drawn scrutiny for interfering with bicycle tracks, footpaths, green spaces, slip roads, and parking zones. Critical areas include slip roads at Junction 45 in Sector 38D and Junction 33 on Dakshin Marg in Sector 35A.Dark stretches and damaged infrastructureNon-functional streetlights have left tracks along Sukhna Path, Himalaya Marg, and Maloya poorly lit, with missing or broken fittings prolonging outages.“A poorly lit cycle track becomes difficult to use after dark. Regular inspections and timely replacement of damaged fittings are essential,” said Manisha Jha, a cycling enthusiast from Sector 40.Damaged streetlight poles near the Grain Market on Chandi Path in Sector 26 require structural repairs and protective measures to withstand vehicle impacts.Authorities face mounting pressure to clear obstructions and repair damaged tracks as commuters struggle with daily hazards.A UT official defended the upkeep, stating: “The administration regularly maintains the tracks. articles.title: The Gambia to pay reparations to ex-dictator’s victims from sale of US mansion
articles.summary: The Gambia confirmed it received $2.5m from the sale of a US mansion belonging to former president Jammeh.
articles.body:
Gambian authorities have announced that funds from the sale of the country’s former president’s mansion in the United States would be used to pay reparations to victims of his rule.

The Gambia Reparations Commission confirmed Tuesday that it received just more than $2.5m from the sale of a property in the wealthy Washington, DC suburb of Potomac, Maryland, belonging to ex-President Yahya Jammeh .

The commission, which was set up to compensate victims of abuses committed during Jammeh’s 22-year rule ending in 2017, said in a statement that “the funds were deposited directly into the Reparations Fund account at the Central Bank of The Gambia and shall only be utilized for the payment of reparations”.

“The Commission is committed to ensuring that the funds are managed responsibly, transparently and accountably, with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors,” it added.

Jammeh currently lives in Equatorial Guinea, after he was forced out under pressure from The Gambia’s West African neighbours following his 2016 election loss to current President Adama Barrow.

He is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.

A commission of inquiry estimated that between 240 and 250 victims were killed by Jammeh’s forces in the former British colony of two million people.

President Barrow said in a statement that his government would heed any recommendations by official auditors on how the funds would be allocated to victims.

The US Justice Department filed a civil forfeiture complaint in 2020 alleging that the property was bought with proceeds of corruption. A court ordered its forfeiture in 2022.

The property, it asserted, was purchased through a trust set up by Jammeh’s wife.

The US Justice Department had announced in September that it would return the funds from the mansion sale to The Gambia.

articles.title: NAACP requests Pennsylvania home pull Halloween decorations hanging fake bodies from trees
articles.summary: Bucks County NAACP said Halloween decorations featuring fake bodies hung from trees evoke lynching and racial terror and urged the owner to remove them.
articles.body: The Bucks County NAACP called for a Pennsylvania home to remove its Halloween decorations on Thursday, accusing the display of carrying a "painful historical significance" for Black Americans. In a statement on social media, the Bucks County NAACP reported on a complaint earlier this month regarding a home featuring fake bodies wrapped in black body bags and hung from trees. The organization felt "deeply concerned" over this display, remarking that "something can be legally permissible and still be profoundly harmful." "For Black Americans, this imagery carries a painful historical significance rooted in lynching and racial terror," Bucks County NAACP said. "While we recognize that Halloween decorations are often intended to frighten or shock, intent does not erase impact." DHS RIPS HOUSTON HALLOWEEN DISPLAY DEPICTING HANGING OF ICE AGENTS, DEMANDS 'SANCTUARY POLITICIANS' STAND DOWN The organization has spoken with the Bristol Borough council on the matter, but it emphasized that it was focused more on "voluntary reconsideration of the display" rather than forcibly removing the decorations. "This is not about restricting Halloween celebrations or freedom of expression. It is about historical awareness, empathy, and respect for our neighbors. We cannot change our history, but we can choose how we respond when that history is invoked in our communities today," the statement read. In a statement to Fox News Digital, the Bucks County NAACP confirmed the council has responded to their concerns and has spoken to the homeowner at the heart of the conflict. The organization also clarified that it has not advocated for government censorship or asserted that the resident committed a crime with the display. "We are encouraging the homeowner to voluntarily reconsider the display and are interested in working with borough leadership on opportunities for community education and constructive dialogue. Ultimately, our goal is not to assign motives or create division. It is to encourage historical awareness, empathy, and respect for the experiences of others. We cannot begin to bridge divides we refuse to acknowledge," Bucks County NAACP President Adrienne King told Fox News Digital. TEXAS WOMAN'S STRIPPER-THEMED HALLOWEEN DISPLAY LEADS TO CLASH WITH HOMEOWNERS ASSOCIATION King also said that since the story has gotten attention, she has received several personal calls and messages about similar displays outside of Bucks County, suggesting "the issue extends beyond one homeowner or one community." In a comment to Fox News Digital, Bristol Borough Manager James Dillon confirmed that he and other members of the council spoke to the homeowner. The homeowner informed them that the display was not meant to offend and that he has no intention of removing it. articles.title: How the UK's hottest summer has affected autumn leaves
articles.summary: The UK's hottest summer on record has caused some trees to shed their leaves early, but experts say spectacular autumn colours could still be on the way.
articles.body:
This year's display of autumn leaves could look rather different following the UK's hottest summer on record.

Months of heat and drought have put trees under stress, causing some to shed their leaves earlier than usual in a phenomenon known as a "false autumn".

Experts say this could mean a more varied display of autumn colours, with some trees losing their leaves prematurely while others are yet to change colour.

However, some trees could still produce spectacular shades of red, orange and gold.

The UK's record-breaking summer brought prolonged periods of heat and dry weather, with some parts of the country particularly affected by drought.

Kevin Martin, Head of Tree Collections at Royal Bontanic Gardens, Kew, said: "Following the UK's hottest summer on record, we may not see the usual blaze of autumn colour arrive all at once this year."

Many trees, particularly in southern England, have already shed their leaves prematurely. This happens when trees respond to heat and drought stress by dropping their leaves early to conserve water.

"False autumns are a warning sign. Trees can live for hundreds of years, but they are increasingly under pressure from a rapidly changing climate," Martin said.

However, some trees could still produce spectacular autumn colours.

"Recent rainfall could still bring a strong display from individual trees in October, and some species may put on an even more impressive show than usual," he added.

Forestry England says autumn colours are developing at different rates across the country's woodlands.

Its Autumn Leaf Watch tracker , external showed early signs of yellow, orange and red in forests including the New Forest, Delamere Forest, Wyre Forest and the Forest of Dean at the end of September.

Silver birch, rowan and horse chestnut were among the species already changing colour, while many oak and beech trees remained predominantly green.

Some western and central forests were showing stronger early signs of autumn colour, although this does not necessarily mean they will have the most vibrant displays later in the season.

Chris Sorensen, Forest Management Advisor at Forestry England, told BBC Weather: "Rather than a single moment when autumn arrives everywhere, colour tends to develop at different rates depending on local weather, elevation, tree species and site conditions."

"That's why visitors to the nation's forests can see very different stages of autumn even between forests that are relatively close together."

What weather conditions are ideal for autumn foliage?

A mixture of sunny days and cooler nights generally provides the best conditions for a colourful autumn display.

"The ideal autumn conditions are generally a mix of sunny days and cooler nights, without prolonged periods of strong winds or heavy rain," Sorensen said.

"Those conditions allow colours to develop gradually and help leaves stay on the trees for longer, extending the display."

This year, however, the exceptionally dry summer faced by some parts of the country has left trees parched.

UK trees "desperately need more rain following months of drought", Martin said.

articles.title: Ali G is back. But is Sacha Baron Cohen's character past its sell-by date?
articles.summary: Borat and Bruno creator Sacha Baron Cohen returns as Ali G, more than two decades after the release of Ali G Indahouse.
articles.body:
"This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.

Behind him, hundreds of fans cram onto a London Underground escalator, all wearing Ali G's trademark yellow shell suit and skullcap. Baron Cohen shouts the character's catchphrases through a megaphone, with the crowd enthusiastically finishing each one.

Earlier this month, more than 300 fans attended an official Ali G lookalike competition, ferried around London on an open-top bus that stopped at landmarks including Big Ben, Leicester Square and Covent Garden.

The stunt was promotion for an upcoming sequel to 2002 film Ali G Indahouse - called Ali G: Who iz I? - which hits cinemas on Friday.

But not everyone is excited about the return of Baron Cohen's comedy character. Critics have long accused the actor of perpetuating racial stereotypes with Ali G, and criticism of the upcoming sequel has gained traction online, with social media posts from comedians, content creators and film fans attracting thousands of likes and comments.

Among them is singer and presenter Jordan Stephens, who has posted multiple TikToks criticising the franchise's return. And last month, discussing the film's trailer on the Jeremy Vine show, Labour MP Paulette Hamilton called the character racist. She said she believed Baron Cohen would not get away with portraying any other racial group "in the way he has done with the black community".

Baron Cohen has not directly addressed criticism of the character's return, and did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

However, he acknowledged an inevitable backlash when he first announced the sequel, writing on X: "In an age where a comedian's career can be ended by a single un-PC joke, I thought I'd play it safe and bring this guy back."

Recently, he shared a video posted to a newly created Instagram account, in which a grey-haired academic urged viewers to boycott the upcoming film. The character appeared to be Baron Cohen in prosthetic makeup.

Has Ali G passed his sell-by date? Or are racial stereotypes, and those who believe them, the true butt of the joke?

Alternatively, as some critics argue, is the whole thing simply not very funny?

The character of Ali G rose to fame through a series of deadpan TV interviews with figures including Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed and the Beckhams, from which catchphrases such as "Booyakasha" and "Is it because I is black?" entered popular culture.

But some critics say these catchphrases have since been appropriated by others in a real-life context to mock black people and dismiss their concerns.

Comedian Dane Baptiste, the first black British comic nominated for an Edinburgh Comedy Award, remembers hearing Ali G catchphrases everywhere during the character's noughties heyday. "A lot of the time, I would hear people using phrases like 'Is it because I is black?' or 'Booyakasha'," he recalls.

"Even taking the phrase 'Is it because I is black?'... that was used to the point of caricature, whereby, whenever black people experienced actual grievances relating to systemic and institutional racism, it was reduced to this catchphrase."

Baptiste believes the character, which he calls a "black caricature", is returning at a time when black creatives are being "starved of opportunities".

The controversy around Ali G is not new. When the Ali G Indahouse movie was released in 2002, protesters gathered at its Leicester Square premiere and organiser Peter Akinti branded the character the "new Al Jolson", a 1920s entertainer who used to perform in blackface.

Little is known about the plot of the Ali G sequel beyond the character discovering his girlfriend Julie is pregnant and travelling to America to interview a slew of unsuspecting real-world participants, including American physicist Alan Lightman and retired Army General C Stewart Rodeheaver, who appears in the film's trailer.

When Ali G first arrived on our screens, characters like him were far more common, says social psychologist Amy Kean. She argues they are no longer "culturally relevant".

"Ali G, Little Britain, Catherine Tate, all of those comedians and sketch shows, they made the voice the joke," says Kean, who has written on accentism, drawing from her experiences being teased for her Essex accent.

"I remember going to school in the 90s and people would take the piss out of anyone whose voice wasn't exactly the same as everyone else's."

Baron Cohen has in the past suggested that his character had a knack for pushing powerful interviewees into uncomfortable territory by playing with biases and expectations.

Speaking on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert in 2020, Baron Cohen reflected on interviewing Donald Trump for Da Ali G Show, and recalled how the programme's producer was a well-spoken Englishman who Trump had assumed would be conducting the interview.

"I remember Donald Trump looking at me, and I'm wearing a sweatsuit," Baron Cohen said. "His face dropped. He was immediately furious that he was going to have to speak to somebody from a lower-class borough rather than this rather astute Etonian producer."

Writing for Time magazine in 2020, Baron Cohen said: "By getting people to reveal what they really believe, I have at times exposed the ignorance, bigotry and conspiratorial delusions that often lurk just below the surface of our modern lives."

Yet, when discussing the upcoming sequel on CBS on Tuesday, Baron Cohen's "primary objective" appeared less ideological - to "get people to laugh really hard". Though he added that "smuggled in there is a bit of satire".

The actor is no stranger to putting himself in potentially dangerous situations for his comedy. In a previous film, he infiltrated a gun rally, disguised as a "right-wing singer", while secretly wearing a bulletproof vest.

Once members of the crowd realised they were being mocked, Baron Cohen was escorted into a getaway vehicle as an angry crowd "started pounding on the vehicle with their fists".

Judging by Baron Cohen's description of the upcoming film, there may be further potential for danger. He told CBS he wanted to examine "conspiracies and lies" and test whether "we, in a matter of hours, could turn intelligent people who believed in the theory of race replacement into murderers".

Colton Dunn, one of the film's black writers, questioned why Baron Cohen would put himself in danger, where interview subjects might react violently, if his intentions were racist.

"From my point of view, Ali G is not a racist character. Ali G is a tool to expose racists," Dunn told Deadline.

"That's why I signed on. I wouldn't sign on to work with somebody that I thought was racist, that's against everything that I've done," he added.

Almost 25 years on, Ali G still has loyal fans - especially in his "home town" of Staines, in Surrey.

Staines-upon-Thames resident Alex Balkan, who campaigned for a statue of Ali G in the town, says the character remains a source of local pride.

While acknowledging not everyone welcomes the proposal, he says Ali G put Staines on the map.

"Everyone knows about us because of Ali G, and many of us wear that as a badge of pride," he says. "It's a great conversation starter. It feels nice that people know about your town."

Asked about accusations of racial stereotyping, Balkan believes the character is designed to be seen as a white man attempting to put on a stereotypical gangster persona, rather than to poke fun at black culture itself.

One of the character's defenders is one of his most famous prank victims, politician Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg.

"It is clever, satirical humour which makes the country, and many of us look foolish, and that's no bad thing," Sir Jacob posted on his social media.

While some argue that audiences may have moved on from Ali G, supporters of the character contend that objections to his return reflect growing concerns about creative freedom in comedy. Balkan goes further, arguing that people today are more easily offended than they were two decades ago.

"This excessive zeal of political correctness, of left-wing po-facery, is crazy," Sir Jacob said. "It's a joke, it's comedy and it is poking fun at society as it is, as the best comedy often does."

It would be unwise to judge the film before audiences have seen it. But the controversy surrounding its release suggests that, more than two decades after Ali G first appeared, the debate over who exactly is being laughed at is far from settled.

articles.title: I left top secret files on the train - you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life
articles.summary: Top civil servant Richard Jackson recounts that fateful day and how he recovered in the aftermath.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains a reference to suicide

It was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late.

He had left highly classified documents on the train.

The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation.

Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath to BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life.

Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university.

"We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career.

"My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility.

"I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."

He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.

Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.

Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret".

In hindsight, Jackson says he should have phoned the Cabinet Office and asked someone to collect the documents securely.

But he puts what he did next down to "maybe a bit of self-preservation".

"Maybe if I get them back, no one else will ever know."

He put the top secret papers in a bright orange cardboard folder and sat on the train the next morning thinking over and over "do not forget this".

He got off the train and walked briskly towards Whitehall. Then he "realised I hadn't got the folder... it just felt for a moment like the world had stopped."

Jackson went to every station the train stopped at and asked whether someone had handed a folder in. Nothing.

"I was frantic. Everything, every movement felt very jerky... I felt sick."

He didn't outwardly break down until he saw Maddie: "I told her I'd ruined our lives. She just held me. She told me it would be all right and we'd get through this."

At work the next day, Jackson discovered the documents had been found and handed to the BBC.

Jackson says his first sense was "relief in that the papers were back somewhere safe" before the realisation "it was now going to be public".

"I was the main story on the 6 o'clock news that night. And they [the Civil Service] suspended me, pending an investigation."

Jackson hid away at home. One lunchtime, Maddie found him sitting cross-legged on the sofa sobbing.

"I'd spent the morning trying to find a painless way to die," he says, "I've often thought what would have happened if she hadn't come home that lunchtime… but I guess I'll never know.

"We spent that afternoon talking… and I think that was the first time where I thought, 'if I'm going to get through this, I can't do it on my own'."

The Cabinet Office found it was an act of gross misconduct and demoted him three grades. He was charged under the Official Secrets Act, avoided jail, and was fined £2,500.

On paper it was over. But Jackson could not shake the feelings of shame, regret and humiliation. He credits the many people who cared about him for helping him piece his life back together. "I fixed very little myself. Lots of people fixed me."

After returning to the MoD in an HR role, then moving to the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to work on the Olympics, Jackson left the Civil Service and worked for the Samaritans. He then took on a role running a team of analysts looking at global terror risk, and started training as a life coach in his spare time.

When he was made redundant, he set up a coaching company, NewDay, which helps people cope with the stress of handling distressing material.

"I could tell my story... and there'd be a point to it. There'd be a reason for what I did."

He wants people to know there is a way back from the biggest mistake of your life.

"You can be in a really bad place, and you can still stand up, and you can get through it and there are ways to help yourself do that and get help."

Asked if he's forgiven himself he says no - but he is happy again.

Maddie is happy too that he no longer works 100 hour weeks. "My life is not defined by my career and I'm more present at home," he says.

"I am much more appreciative of how lucky I am to have magical people in my life."

Made a mistake? Here are ways to help you recover

Richard Jackson has shared steps that helped him move through his traumatic episode:

Get your thoughts out of your head. In a dark place, your mind jumps from "I made a terrible mistake" to "I am a worthless person" at the speed of thought. Writing it down or talking to someone slows things down to give you a chance to notice the illogical leaps.

Continue activities you enjoy. When you feel unworthy, you stop doing the things that lift you up. Work out what they are - the gym, a book, a long walk - and make them non-negotiable fixtures in your routine.

Remember your worth and your success. I keep an evidence board by my desk with notes of things I have achieved and kind things people have said. It's a tangible reminder that I am not that mistake, I am so much more.

Find your critical friend. You need someone who is your cheerleader but will also call you out when you let good habits slip. Anyone who is truly on your side.

Work out what you can fix, and what you can't. If you've caused harm, take responsibility: apologise and put things right where you can. But don't assume responsibility for things that were never yours to carry.

Don't confuse your worst moment with the whole story of your life. You are not that mistake. You are still the person who existed before it, and there can still be a person after it whom you haven't met.

If you or someone you know has been affected by a traumatic experience or is suffering from emotional distress, there is support on the BBC Action Line website.

articles.title: Tighter rules planned to protect people from botched cosmetic surgery
articles.summary: There will be restrictions on who can carry out procedures and fines for those who flout the law, in England in 2027.
articles.body:
Only properly trained professionals will be allowed to offer high-risk cosmetic procedures like liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), vampire facials and chemical peels, under long-awaited government plans for England in 2027.

The government said it wanted to "drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market" and shield people from treatments "that can go badly wrong".

Currently, there are no restrictions over who can carry out these 'no scalpel' procedures, which can harm or kill if not performed safely.

Under the new rules, high-risk procedures for under-18s will also be banned, and rogue providers will face new criminal offences and fixed fines of up to £4,000.

The government began consulting on changes to the cosmetic surgery industry in 2023, but there have been calls for stricter regulations for many years.

It comes following horror stories of procedures reportedly carried out in Airbnbs, hotel rooms, garden sheds and even public toilets, by "cosmetic cowboys" .

Women have told the BBC of dangerous complications , pain and permanent scarring after treatment by rogue operators.

Alice Webb, a mother-of-five from Gloucestershire, died within hours of getting a liquid Brazilian butt lift in 2024.

That same year, Sasha Dean, from Bedfordshire, was left in a coma after receiving a liquid BBL.

A BBL is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which dermal fillers are injected into the buttocks to alter their size or shape.

Some of Sasha's treatment took place in a private house and she ended up developing sepsis.

She told BBC News: "Very quickly it turned into a complete nightmare.

"I had a heart attack, one of my lungs had collapsed, my kidneys were failing. My body was just completely shutting down."

Fillers injected into parts of the body other than the face, like liquid BBLs, will be legally defined as cosmetic surgical procedures, meaning only doctors could perform the surgery

High-risk non-surgical or wellbeing treatments, including deep chemical peels, vampire facials, dermal micro-coring and some laser procedures would be restricted to doctors, dentists and some nurses, midwives and pharmacists who have been trained

Cosmetic surgery and risky treatments will be banned for under 18s - lip fillers and face Botox on children has already been stopped

The dark side of the Brazilian butt lift boom

Vampire facials involve drawing a patient's blood and then separating out platelet-rich plasma from it using a centrifuge. The plasma is then injected back into the face through tiny needle punctures

Dermal micro-coring involves removing tiny sections of skin using thin hollow needles, small enough to allow scarless healing

Chemical peels are skin resurfacing procedures that use a chemical solution to remove the top layers of skin

Health Minister Karin Smyth said: "We want to drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market and raise standards across the board, giving reputable businesses a fair chance to thrive by helping people identify safe, qualified providers they can trust."

The British Beauty Council said the government should be congratulated for tackling the issue head-on.

But Mr Keith Allison, from the Royal College of Surgeons of England, said the consultation was "long overdue" and, while welcome, the proposals did not go far enough.

"Ministers must ensure they do not create a new loophole in patient protection by regulating non-surgical cosmetic procedures more robustly than cosmetic surgery itself.

"A doctor should not be able to carry out cosmetic surgery simply because they hold a medical license."

The government will now ask doctors, businesses, regulators, the public and other experts for their say on the draft rules, before plans go through parliament in spring 2027.

A licensing scheme for Botox clinics in England to improve safety standards has already been announced.

In Scotland, laws passed in March mean cosmetic procedures must be performed by, or alongside, certain healthcare professionals in a registered setting. Non-surgical procedures are banned for under 18s.

There are no dedicated regulations around cosmetic procedures in Wales or Northern Ireland.

articles.title: Guatemalan man sentenced to 30 years for smuggling tragedy that killed 53 people in Texas
articles.summary: The trailer’s air conditioning wouldn’t blow cool air to the people trapped inside during the sweltering, three-hour ride in June 2022 from the border city of Laredo to San Antonio, authorities said.
articles.body: A federal judge on Tuesday sentenced a Guatemalan man extradited to the U.S. over his role in a 2022 human smuggling attempt that ended in the deaths of 53 migrants who had been transported in a sweltering tractor-trailer in Texas. U.S. and Guatemalan prosecutors called Rigoberto Román Miranda-Orozco's sentencing another step toward justice in one of the deadliest smuggling attempts along the U.S.-Mexico border. Miranda-Orozco, 39, was sentenced to 30 years in prison after admitting to arranging travel and accommodations for two people who died and another who was seriously injured. Nearly 20 people in the U.S. and Guatemala have been convicted since the discovery of the abandoned trailer full of bodies horrified communities accustomed to seeing their young people leave, trying to flee poverty or violence in Central America and Mexico. “It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth,” U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a news conference following the sentencing. People tried to ‘claw their way out’ of a trailer with no air conditioning The trailer’s air conditioning malfunctioned and would not blow cool air to the people trapped inside during the sweltering, three-hour ride in June 2022 from the border city of Laredo to San Antonio, authorities said. Prosecutors have said migrants paid up to $15,000 each to be taken across the U.S. border. When the abandoned trailer was opened on a remote San Antonio back road, 48 migrants were dead. Another 16 were taken to hospitals, where five more died. Simmons said investigators found clothing passengers had shed to cool off and claw marks on the trailer’s walls. “They were literally trying to claw their way out,” he said. Twenty-one of those who died were from Guatemala, Simmons said. Other defendants still await sentencing U.S. District Judge Orlando Garcia sentenced Miranda-Orozco, who was arrested in Guatemala in 2024 and extradited to the U.S. the following year. He pleaded guilty in July to conspiracy to bring a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting bringing a migrant into the U.S. resulting in serious bodily injury, prosecutors said. Simmons said prosecutors in Guatemala were integral in securing convictions for Miranda-Orozco and others. Guatemalan Attorney General Gabriel García Luna attended Tuesday's news conference in Texas. Last year, Felipe Orduna-Torres, described by prosecutors as the leader of the smuggling operations inside the U.S., was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. Armando Gonzales-Ortega, his top assistant, was sentenced to 83 years. Sentencing dates have been set for more people, including the truck’s driver. The tragedy is the deadliest among those that have claimed thousands of lives in recent decades as people attempt to cross the U.S. border from Mexico. Ten migrants died in 2017 after they were trapped inside a truck parked at a Walmart in San Antonio. In 2003, the bodies of 19 migrants were found in a sweltering truck southeast of San Antonio.

images.caption: Police and other first responders work the scene where officials say dozens of people have been found dead and multiple others were taken to hospitals with heat-related illnesses after a tractor-trailer containing suspected migrants was found on June 27, 2022, in San Antonio.

articles.title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
articles.summary: Investigative genetic genealogy can help hunt down criminals but raises worries over privacy.
articles.body:
Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.

The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.

The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.

For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.

The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.

Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.

They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.

Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.

Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member.

"That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.

It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.

Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."

The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved.

It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations.

Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map."

Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect.

However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed.

DNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases.

One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.

Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.

They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.

The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.

This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.

But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."

Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique."

"But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.

While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data.

"There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.

A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."

Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.

While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.

The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.

articles.title: NATO to send additional patrol planes to Black Sea after drone attacks
articles.summary: The alliance announces the deployment after a series of deadly drone attacks in the region.
articles.body:
NATO is deploying additional patrol aircraft and intelligence personnel to the Black Sea, a spokesman for the alliance said, after a series of deadly drone attacks in the region widely blamed on Russia but denied by the Kremlin.

“Allies have or will send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, explosive exploitation teams, intelligence personnel, drones and more to the Black Sea,” said Colonel Martin O’Donnell on Tuesday.

“The most important thing we can do, however, is to increase our situational awareness in the region through increased sensors and data sharing,” he added.

NATO, along with Bulgaria and Romania, has not directly attributed the recent spate of attacks to any country. Military analysts have said Russia almost certainly carried out the attacks but Moscow has not acknowledged any responsibility.

In an attack on October 5, Romania reported two people dead after their ship caught fire and sank in Black Sea waters. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of being responsible.

The announcement came after NATO’s main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, discussed security in the Black Sea at the alliance’s Brussels headquarters.

“NATO has already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone capabilities,” spokeswoman Allison Hart said earlier in a post on X.

The European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas on Tuesday said that “six attacks in 10 days by suspected Russian drones marks a dangerous and unacceptable escalation”, adding that the Kremlin likely sought to choke off revenue to Kyiv from grain exports.

Kallas warned that the latest strikes were adding to a “perfect storm” facing global food supplies already being battered by droughts in multiple regions and the war in the Middle East.

Last week, seven sailors were reported missing after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine.

At least five other cargo vessels were hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring NATO member Bulgaria over the previous 10 days, with at least 23 sailors reported missing or dead .
